finding.claim: @inspectFile fails open: any exec error (NUL byte in argv, argv over MAX_ARG_STRLEN) is treated as 'no match', so an attacker-controlled value that makes exec fail is never scanned.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled variable value, e.g. ARGS value with %00 (url.go:67 decodes it to 0x00) or raw REQUEST_BODY containing 0x00, or a value >128KiB on Linux.
finding.sink: exec.CommandContext(ctx, o.path, value).CombinedOutput() at inspect_file.go:53-54; error swallowed at 55-57 returning false.

trace.note: queryUnescape writes byte(hi<<4|lo) for %XX, so %00 becomes a NUL byte in the ARGS value
ExtractGetArguments stores the decoded value into ARGS_GET via AddGetRequestArgument
Evaluate receives the value unchanged
value passed as argv to the external scanner
Go's syscall layer rejects argv strings containing NUL with EINVAL, so CombinedOutput returns an error and the scanner never runs
err != nil (also ctx timeout) returns false, which SecRule treats as no match, so the request is allowed

finding.guards_checked: Only the 10s context timeout (inspect_file.go:50). No NUL check, no argv length check, no distinction between exec failure and a clean result. The operator is built on all non-TinyGo targets (build tag at line 4). Impact depends on the admin having @inspectFile on a variable an attacker can populate (ARGS, REQUEST_BODY, headers). FILES_TMPNAMES paths cannot contain NUL, so that case is not affected.

finding.claim: Query-string arguments beyond ArgumentLimit (default 1000) are silently dropped, so a payload placed after the 1000th parameter never reaches ARGS_GET/ARGS.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled request URI query string with more than 1000 '&'-separated pairs.
finding.sink: ARGS_GET population: tx.variables.argsGet.Add at transaction.go:776, skipped by the limit check at 772-775.

trace.note: ProcessURI calls ExtractGetArguments(parsedURL.RawQuery)
ParseQuery builds the full map with no count limit
loops every key/value and calls AddGetRequestArgument
checkArgumentLimit: argsGet.Len() >= WAF.ArgumentLimit returns early
the argument is dropped; the only signal is a debug-level log at 773
ArgumentLimit defaults to 1000

finding.guards_checked: Limit is enforced (ARGS_GET is capped). But the drop is silent: no REQBODY_ERROR-style flag, no interruption, only a debug log. REQUEST_URI_RAW and REQUEST_LINE still contain the full query, so rules on those variables still fire. Rules that only look at ARGS/ARGS_GET/QUERY_STRING miss the payload. Behaviour is a fail-open design choice and should be documented or flagged as a variable.

finding.claim: ArgumentLimit is never applied to POST/body arguments. AddPostRequestArgument (transaction.go:780) has no callers, and the urlencoded, multipart and JSON processors write to ArgsPost directly. An attacker can create an unbounded number of ARGS_POST entries, up to the request body limit.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled urlencoded, multipart or JSON request body.
finding.sink: ArgsPost population: argsCol.Set(k, vs) at urlencoded.go:29 and the rule-evaluation loops over ARGS_POST.

trace.note: ParseQuery builds a map of every key in the body with no count limit
argsCol.Set writes each key directly, bypassing checkArgumentLimit
multipart fields use postCol.Add directly, also unlimited
JSON keys use col.SetIndex directly, also unlimited
AddPostRequestArgument, the only limit-checked POST path, has no callers (repo-wide grep)
RequestBodyLimit default is 134217728 (128 MiB), so up to ~tens of millions of pairs can be created

finding.guards_checked: Body size limit only (default 128 MiB, Reject action at waf.go:332). No argument-count check. The documented ArgumentLimit is effectively not enforced for body arguments. This is a resource-exhaustion (CPU/memory during rule evaluation) issue, not a bypass.

finding.claim: FILES_SIZES is keyed by the attacker-chosen filename and written with SetIndex(index 0), which overwrites on duplicate names. A large file can be hidden from size-based rules by a later part with the same filename and a small size.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled multipart body with two file parts sharing the same filename.
finding.sink: fileSizesCol.SetIndex(filename, 0, size) at multipart.go:100, read by rules on FILES_SIZES.

trace.note: filesCol.Add records the filename; FILES is appended, so both parts are listed
SetIndex(filename,0,size) with an existing key
len(values) > index, so the default branch runs
c.data[key][0] = av overwrites the first file's size with the second file's size (for example 10 MB replaced by 1 byte)

finding.guards_checked: FILES_COMBINED_SIZE (multipart.go:102) is cumulative and correct. File contents are still written to FILES_TMPNAMES and inspected by @inspectFile/rules, so the impact is limited to rules keyed on FILES_SIZES (for example a max-file-size rule). Map keys are lowercased for case-insensitive collections, so 'A.bin' and 'a.bin' collide too.

finding.claim: When url.ParseRequestURI fails, ProcessURI never extracts query arguments (ExtractGetArguments is only called on the success branch), so ARGS_GET and QUERY_STRING are empty while the raw URI, including the query, still reaches REQUEST_FILENAME/REQUEST_BASENAME and REQUEST_URI.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled request line that Go's ParseRequestURI rejects, e.g. an invalid percent-escape in the path such as /index.php%zz?id=<payload>.
finding.sink: ARGS_GET / QUERY_STRING population is skipped; the payload in the query is not parsed into ARGS.

trace.note: url.ParseRequestURI(uri) runs on the raw request target
on err, urlencodedError is set (no rule blocks on it by default) and path = uri
requestURI is set to the raw URI
ExtractGetArguments is only on the success branch, so it is skipped here
queryString is set from query, which is still empty on this branch

finding.guards_checked: urlencodedError is set but no default rule denies on it. Go's net/http server applies the same ParseRequestURI and rejects such requests with 400, so this only matters for a backend that accepts invalid path escapes and parses the query (for example some non-Go servers behind the WAF). Confidence is medium and depends on the deployment.
